introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 3 (0790), Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section (Section One: Logic; Section Two: Philosophical Problems). Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion, as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Q2(a)(i) : « normal » est lu comme le complémentaire de « abnormal » et « unwise » comme celui de « wise ». Le résultat est la contraposée partielle (par limitation) d'une E : valide en logique traditionnelle, avec import existentiel de la classe des personnes anormales (vérifié avec Python : les contre-modèles n'existent que lorsque cette classe est vide).

Q2(a)(ii) : I vers O de mêmes termes (subcontraires), illicite ; vérifié avec Python (contre-modèles). Les deux mots « logical relations » sont traités comme « relation entre la prémisse et la conclusion » (obversion, conversion, contraposition, subcontrariété).

Q2(b)(i) : la mineure est la prémisse qui contient « students » ; pour que le moyen terme (learners) soit non distribué dans une O, il doit en être le SUJET (« Some learners are not students »). Argument AOO-4, invalide, contre-modèle vérifié avec Python. Convention des ordres d'enthymème : 2e ordre = prémisse mineure supprimée.

Q2(d) : le sujet imprime des parenthèses incomplètes pour (ii) « [A v~Z) ≡ (Y · B)] » et (iii) « [~C · ~Z) v (B · C)] » ; elles sont lues « [(A v ~Z) ≡ (Y · B)] » et « [(~C · ~Z) v (B · C)] ». Résultats (i) vrai, (ii) faux, (iii) vrai, vérifiés avec Python ; la lecture alternative ~(C · ~Z) en (iii) donnerait la même valeur (vrai).

Q2(c)(ii) : le sophisme est donné comme appel à la force (argumentum ad baculum) ; la menace est implicite (« if you want to secure a good pass »), une lecture « corruption / abus d'autorité » est mentionnée dans le corrigé.
Points : (a) 2 x 2 = 4 ; (b) 2 x 3 = 6 ; (c) 3 x 3 = 9 ; (d) 3 x 2 = 6 ; total 25, conforme aux 25 marks imprimés.

Numérotation : le sujet imprime « 3. », « 4. », « 5. », « 6. » ; les questions 1 et 2 n'ont pas de numéro lisible (la question 1 est annoncée par le passage de lecture, la question 2 par un point isolé devant « (a) »). Numéros déduits de la suite 1 à 6 ; la section Logic compte donc trois questions, la section Philosophical Problems trois.

Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section » (quatre questions au total, deux par section). Section One (Logic) : questions 1 à 3 ; Section Two (Philosophical Problems) : questions 4 à 6. `regles_choix` porte une règle `parmi 2 sur 3` par section ; la règle « 4 en tout » est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : le corrigé est une réponse modèle rédigée ; la logique est recalculée avec Python (itertools, modèles d'ensembles), la philosophie est donnée de mémoire (auteurs et positions de l'histoire établie de la philosophie, sans citation littérale, titre d'ouvrage, date ni numéro de page). À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné de 4 pages (page de garde, Section One pages 2 et 3, Section Two page 4) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo, sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024, Philosophy, Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), Subject Code 0790, trois heures.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**2.** (a) State the logical relations in the following inferences and determine whether they are valid or illicit:

(i) No abnormal persons are wise persons, so some unwise persons are not normal persons

(ii) Given that some non-men are non-women, it follows that some non-men are not non-women

(2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Complementary terms are used: "normal" is read as "non-abnormal" and "unwise" as "non-wise".

**(i) (2 marks).** Let $A$ = abnormal persons and $W$ = wise persons. The premise is an E-proposition, "No $A$ are $W$". The conclusion is an O-proposition, "Some non-$W$ are not non-$A$". The relation is **contraposition by limitation** (partial contraposition) of an E-proposition, obtained in three steps:

1. No abnormal persons are wise persons. (E: No $A$ are $W$)
2. By **obversion**: All abnormal persons are unwise persons. (A: All $A$ are non-$W$)
3. By **conversion by limitation** (per accidens): Some unwise persons are abnormal persons. (I: Some non-$W$ are $A$)
4. By **obversion**: Some unwise persons are not normal persons. (O: Some non-$W$ are not non-$A$)

Verdict: the inference is **valid**. (In traditional logic, step 3 assumes that the class of abnormal persons is not empty; with this assumption no case makes the premise true and the conclusion false. Under the modern reading, which gives no existential import to the universal form, it holds only if there is at least one abnormal person.)

**(ii) (2 marks).** The premise "Some non-men are non-women" is an **I-proposition**; the conclusion "Some non-men are not non-women" is the **O-proposition** with the same subject and predicate. I and O with the same terms are **subcontraries**: they cannot both be false, but they **can both be true**. If one is true, the other is **undetermined**.

Verdict: the inference is **illicit**: it moves from the truth of one subcontrary to the truth of the other, which the square of opposition does not allow. (Both statements may happen to be true here, but the second does not follow from the first: there are situations in which all non-men are non-women, and then the conclusion is false.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using 'students' as minor term, 'learners' as middle term and 'scholars' as major term:

(i) Construct an argument that commits the fallacy of undistributed middle with an O-proposition as its minor premise

(ii) Construct a second order enthymeme from b (i) above.

(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $S$ = students (minor term), $M$ = learners (middle term), $P$ = scholars (major term). The minor premise is the premise that contains the minor term: it must be an O-proposition. In an O-proposition ("Some $x$ are not $y$") only the **predicate** is distributed. To keep the middle term **undistributed** in the minor premise, $M$ must therefore be the **subject** of the O-proposition: "Some learners are not students". ("Some students are not learners" would distribute "learners", and there would be no fallacy.)

**(i) (3 marks).**

- Major premise (A): All scholars are learners. ($P$ a $M$: the middle term is the predicate of an A-proposition, so it is undistributed)
- Minor premise (O): Some learners are not students. ($M$ o $S$: the middle term is the subject of a particular proposition, so it is undistributed)
- Conclusion (O): Therefore, some students are not scholars. ($S$ o $P$; a negative conclusion, as one premise is negative)

The middle term "learners" is **undistributed in both premises**, so the argument commits the **fallacy of undistributed middle**. Its form is AOO in the fourth figure (AOO-4). Counter-example showing that it is invalid: suppose there is exactly one scholar, who is also a student, and one more learner who is not a student. Both premises are true, but every student is a scholar, so the conclusion is false.

**(ii) (3 marks).** An enthymeme of the **second order** is a syllogism whose **minor premise is suppressed** (first order: major suppressed; third order: conclusion suppressed). Suppressing the minor premise "Some learners are not students" gives:

"All scholars are learners; **therefore some students are not scholars**."

(The suppressed minor premise, "Some learners are not students", is understood by the hearer and can be restored by asking what links "learners" with "students".)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) State the fallacies committed in arguments below:

(i) Aristotle's Traditional Logic is unquestionable because he was the greatest ancient Greek logician.

(ii) "I noticed that you are the labour prefect of the school. I will expect you to tell students to wash my car if you want to secure a good pass in my exams".

(iii) The superb quality of her character can be demonstrated by the fact that I have never heard a word spoken against her.

(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (3 marks). Appeal to authority (argumentum ad verecundiam).** The conclusion, that Aristotle's Traditional Logic cannot be questioned, is supported only by the **prestige of its author**, not by reasons about the logic itself. Being the greatest ancient Greek logician makes Aristotle an important authority, not an infallible one: a theory is justified by the soundness of its arguments, and any logical system, however influential, remains open to examination and revision.

**(ii) (3 marks). Appeal to force (argumentum ad baculum).** The teacher uses the **power he holds over the pupil's result** to obtain an unrelated favour: the sentence "if you want to secure a good pass in my exams" carries an implicit threat (refuse and you will not pass). There is no relevance between washing a car and the quality of an exam script, so the pressure replaces a genuine reason. It is also an abuse of authority (a form of coercion and bribery combined).

**(iii) (3 marks). Argument from ignorance (argumentum ad ignorantiam).** The speaker infers that her character is superb from the **absence of evidence against it** ("I have never heard a word spoken against her"). Not having heard criticism proves nothing: the speaker's information may be limited, people may fear to speak, or the subject may be little known. Lack of evidence of a fault is not evidence of virtue.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Given that A,B,C are true while X,Y,Z are false, compute the truth values of the following statements:

(i) $[(\sim A \cdot \sim X) \equiv (C \cdot \sim B)] \vee (\sim Z \cdot \sim Y)$

(ii) $[(A \vee \sim Z) \equiv (Y \cdot B)] \cdot [\sim(C \supset \sim X) \vee (A \cdot C)]$

(iii) $[(\sim C \cdot \sim Z) \vee (B \cdot C)] \equiv \sim(X \cdot A)$

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Values: $A = B = C = T$ and $X = Y = Z = F$. (Parentheses added where the print shows one missing.)

**(i) (2 marks).** $[(\sim A \cdot \sim X) \equiv (C \cdot \sim B)] \vee (\sim Z \cdot \sim Y)$

- $\sim A = F$ and $\sim X = T$, so $(\sim A \cdot \sim X) = F$.
- $\sim B = F$, so $(C \cdot \sim B) = T \cdot F = F$.
- $F \equiv F = T$.
- $\sim Z = T$ and $\sim Y = T$, so $(\sim Z \cdot \sim Y) = T$.
- Whole: $T \vee T = T$.

The statement is **true**.

**(ii) (2 marks).** $[(A \vee \sim Z) \equiv (Y \cdot B)] \cdot [\sim(C \supset \sim X) \vee (A \cdot C)]$

- Left conjunct: $A \vee \sim Z = T \vee T = T$; $Y \cdot B = F \cdot T = F$; so $T \equiv F = F$.
- Right conjunct (for completeness): $\sim X = T$, $C \supset \sim X = T \supset T = T$, $\sim(C \supset \sim X) = F$, $A \cdot C = T$, so $F \vee T = T$.
- Whole: $F \cdot T = F$ (a conjunction with a false conjunct is false).

The statement is **false**.

**(iii) (2 marks).** $[(\sim C \cdot \sim Z) \vee (B \cdot C)] \equiv \sim(X \cdot A)$

- $\sim C = F$ and $\sim Z = T$, so $(\sim C \cdot \sim Z) = F$; $B \cdot C = T$; so the left side is $F \vee T = T$.
- $X \cdot A = F \cdot T = F$, so $\sim(X \cdot A) = T$.
- Whole: $T \equiv T = T$.

The statement is **true**.
